problem: Seq2seq VLN agents on R2R suffer from exposure bias. Greedy decoders cannot recover once they deviate and often fall into loops. Beam search recovers success rate but explores many full trajectories, so path lengths are huge (hundreds to over 1,000 m on test) and SPL is close to 0.
motivation: All VLN decoding is a search over the navigation graph, yet prior work sits at two extremes: purely local greedy decoding or full global beam sweeps. A practical robot should act greedily but notice when it is lost and backtrack cheaply to the most promising earlier point. The authors observe that SMNA's first action is wrong 40% of the time, and after a first-step mistake greedy success is <30%. This suggests cheap backtracking could recover much of the lost success.
key_idea: Treat action decoding as asynchronous graph search. A frontier priority queue of partial trajectories is scored by a local score (sum of unnormalized action logits). A candidate queue of every visited node is scored by a learned global reranker. This lets the agent move greedily, backtrack to the best frontier point when it detects a mistake, and pick the final goal among all visited nodes.
insight: Unnormalized logits carry alignment-confidence information that softmax normalization discards. Summing logits along a partial trajectory gives the best success rate among local scorers (Table 3: sum-logit SR 56.66 vs mean-logprob 53.85). Naively fusing the progress-monitor score into the frontier score does not help. For choosing the goal, no single signal works well: best single-signal SR on val unseen is 58.75, speaker alone gives 43.68. An MLP over all six signals reaches 64.03, but the oracle is 90.20. So after 40 expansions the agent has usually visited the goal but cannot recognize it, which makes goal recognition, not exploration, the bottleneck. Even one-step backtracking from early mistakes raises success by >10% for those episodes (Fig. on divergence recovery).
method: Three learning signals from a seq2seq follower (SMNA): per-step action logit l_t (dot product of LSTM decoder hidden state with candidate view features), progress monitor p^pm_t (normalized instruction-completion estimate from cell state, previous hidden state, visual input and language attention), and a Speaker seq2seq model scoring P(instruction | trajectory).

Frontier queue Q_F: priority queue of partial trajectories whose last action is proposed but not yet executed. It is sorted by local score L = sum of logits over the trajectory (alternatives ablated: mean, log-prob, fusion with progress monitor).

Global candidate queue Q_C: every visited node/trajectory is a potential destination. It is sorted by global score G, a trained 2-layer MLP (BN→FC→BN→Tanh→FC, 6-d input: sum/mean logits, sum/mean log-probs, progress monitor, speaker score). G is trained with pairwise cross-entropy on 4,378,729 cached pairs; qualified = ending within 3 m of goal.

Backtracking policy: 'exploit' (FAST short) follows the best local action and backtracks to the top of Q_F only when the best action would revisit a node (a loop). 'Explore' (FAST long) always pops the globally best partial trajectory, like an approximation of D* search.
Mental map: caches (node, action)→next-node transitions so revisits are not re-executed and search avoids revisiting nodes unless they lead to high-value unexplored paths.
Stopping criteria: stop when the best local action is STOP (short), or after expanding a fixed budget of M nodes (long); the final answer is argmax_G over Q_C.
Plug-and-play: replaces the greedy decoder of existing agents (SMNA, Speaker-Follower) with no retraining of the follower.

setting.backbone: SMNA follower (full re-implementation; LSTM encoder-decoder with visual-textual co-grounding attention + progress monitor), plus Speaker-Follower speaker model and a small MLP reranker. Also applied to the Speaker-Follower follower.
setting.training_data: R2R train set (follower/speaker as in SMNA / Speaker-Follower). Reranker MLP trained on 4,378,729 candidate pairs cached from running FAST for 40 steps on training data.
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (36 views per viewpoint) + language instruction
setting.action_space: discrete nav-graph viewpoints (panoramic action space) + STOP, with explicit backtracking to previously visited nodes
setting.privileged: none (backtracking moves are physically executed and counted in TL)

numbers_note: Table 1 prints SR/SPL as fractions (e.g. 0.56); these are converted to percent (56). Val-seen cells for FAST (short) are blank in Table 1. Table 3 gives more precise val-unseen numbers for the same sum-of-logits configuration: SR 56.66, SPL 43.64, Len 21.17. Table 4 reports reranker-only success rates after expanding 40 nodes, with 'All' features: Val Seen 71.00, Val Unseen 64.03 (oracle 92.85 / 90.20). These differ slightly from the FAST (long) row in Table 1. The node-budget sweep (SR/SPL vs nodes expanded) and the divergence-recovery analysis are shown only in figures.
results: On R2R test unseen, FAST (short) on top of SMNA reaches SR 54 / SPL 41 (NE 5.14). Greedy SMNA gets 48 / 35 and Speaker-Follower gets 35 / 28, so FAST gives +6 absolute (17% relative) SPL. FAST (long) matches the best beam-search success rate (SMNA beam SR 61) with SR 61 at TL 196.53 vs 373.09. On val unseen it reaches SR 63, above SMNA beam's 57. As a plug-in with no retraining, FAST raises val-unseen SR by +6 for Speaker-Follower (37→43) and by +9 for SMNA (47→56), while SPL also increases slightly.
limitations: The long/explore variant still produces very long trajectories (TL ~200 m, SPL 2-4), so high SR is bought with poor efficiency.

Goal recognition is weak: after 40 expansions the target has been visited >90% of the time, but the reranker picks it only ~64% on val unseen. Progress-monitor fusion into the frontier score did not help.

Evaluated only on R2R's discrete nav-graph with a panoramic action space. Relies on revisitable graph nodes and a follower whose logits are meaningful, and has no continuous-environment or real-robot validation.
